text:
Chapter Sixteen


The next day, Maggie lifted a pile of Dahlia’s rune-covered scraps of paper off Jim’s desk chair and scooted the chair to sit across from her. Dahlia was, almost literally, buried beneath the grading on her desk, which threatened to topple over at any minute.


“Next year, let’s find jobs with teaching assistants and graders,” Dahlia muttered.


“Deal,” Maggie said, knowing very well that they would not be looking for new jobs. Maggie gingerly set a bag containing one of the Bean There, Done That pastries on the top of Dahlia’s towering pile of papers.


“What’s that?” Dahlia asked with her eyes narrowed in suspicion.


“Just bringing my friend some breakfast,” Maggie said with a certain nonchalance that she knew Dahlia would see through immediately.


“You barely remember to feed yourself breakfast.”


“Fine. It’s an apology pastry,” Maggie admitted.


Dahlia tore off a piece of flaky croissant. “What did you do? Is Maggie Linden going to finally live up to her troublemaker reputation?”


Only Dahlia could joke about what happened to Maggie after her ex blew up their relationship and her career at Bryn Ridge and make her laugh. It was one of the things that Maggie loved about her.


Maggie took a deep breath and braced herself. She knew exactly the kind of reaction she was going to get when she revealed why she owed her friend an apology pastry. “I had coffee with Arthur Taliesin last night.”


Dahlia sat up straight, shaking the crumbs off her hands over the pastry bag, and squealed before scooting her chair around the desk. “Coffee coffee?” she asked.


“I don’t know what that means,” Maggie lied.


“You are a linguist; you absolutely know what I mean by a little reduplication. Coffee coffee,” she repeated. “Was it coffee? Or was it coffee coffee?”


“It was a working coffee.” She swore that Dahlia’s face fell slightly. Did she want her to go on a coffee date with Taliesin? “I offered to help him dissipate the pall.”


Dahlia took another bite of croissant and looked at her thoughtfully, but all she said was, “Interesting.”


“What does that mean?”


“It means it’s interesting! I’m frankly surprised he was willing to accept your help.”


Maggie bit her lip. “Well,” she said, pausing. “I might have threatened to investigate the pall by myself if he didn’t let me help.”


Dahlia shoved Maggie playfully. “See! Interesting. When did this happen?”


Maggie cringed. “Last Friday,” she muttered, and Dahlia gasped.


“So that’s what the apology croissant is for.” She dragged the bag back into her lap, an exaggerated pout on her lips. “I can’t believe you waited so long to tell me.”


“I’m sorry! I’ve been trying to come tell you, but I kept missing you.” She knew Dahlia would be distracted by the details, so she told her about Taliesin showing up in their office near death after spending the entire day trying to dissipate the pall on his own.


“The entire day? Was he trying to kill himself?”


Maggie shrugged. “I asked him what he had against help, and he said he didn’t want anyone else getting hurt.” Least of all you. The words were burned in Maggie’s memory, but even though she wasn’t in the habit of lying to Dahlia, there were some things that she still wanted to keep for herself. “And I figure the sooner we get rid of this damn pall, the sooner I get him out of my office. The sooner I can get to working on my translation of Branagh’s Aubade.”


“So, you—and I just want to make sure I’m understanding exactly how this happened—threatened to put yourself in harm’s way if he didn’t let you help him?” When Dahlia worded it that way, it sounded ridiculous.


“No, not that I would put myself in harm’s way,” Maggie clarified. “I told him I would enter the pall for myself and collect my own data.”


“The same pall that nearly killed him? The one he doesn’t want anyone anywhere near?”


“What are you getting at?”


Dahlia shrugged, pursing her lips slightly, but she had a glint in her eye. “Like I said, I’m just trying to get the facts!”


“The facts are that he’s got a serious case of pathological guilt,” Maggie said, and even though she felt a little mean, she added, “and maybe some mommy issues.”


“I’d have mommy issues, too, if my mother was Rowena Taliesin.” Maggie couldn’t imagine growing up in the shadow of someone like Rowena. Rowena, who had come up in academia when it was even more openly hostile to women. Who didn’t let getting pregnant and having a child derail her career, instead raising her son to be just as brilliant, just as ambitious. Rowena was a powerhouse, and every woman in academia had looked to her story at some point for inspiration or commiseration, Maggie and Dahlia included.


Maggie told Dahlia more about their agreement and their meeting at Bean There, Done That; about their walk home together. Dahlia was just as fascinated by the revelation that the other side of Taliesin’s family was local.


Dahlia pushed her glasses up. “So,” she began, steering the conversation in the direction Maggie had been trying to avoid. “What was he like?”


Maggie chose her words carefully. “He’s a different person off campus.” Translation: Kind. Generous. Candid. “I don’t think he scowled the whole time we were there.” Translation: She kept catching him staring at her. Making him laugh was the highlight of her night.


“Maybe he just really hates his job. We’ve all been there,” Dahlia said. “Maybe he finds Dean Clearwater to be insufferable. Honestly, that’s a point in his favor if he does.”


Maggie snorted and tried to drive the conversation away from how Taliesin was off campus. “I didn’t come here just to gossip, I swear.” She held up a file folder she had brought home after her meeting with the alchemist. “Will you look over Taliesin’s runes for me?”


Dahlia took the file folder from Maggie and made some space on her desk to lay out the work. She compared the alchemical equations with the subsequent runes, writing down annotations as she went. She looked over the spell that went wrong and the variations in the dissipation spells Taliesin had tried.


“As annoying as it is, these are pretty perfect,” she finally said. “I thought there was a calculation error from the original spell, but I found the variable that he was factoring in, and it made the spell stronger.”


“I thought the same thing when I looked at them earlier, but I wanted to make sure a runologist saw them.”


Dahlia reached into the paper bag for more of her apology croissant while she went over the calculations in front of her one more time. Dahlia looked up at Maggie, tilting her head to the side. “So, you’re putting your research completely on hold to help him with this? To spend every working hour with Arthur Taliesin, for what could be weeks of your summer?”


“Not every working hour,” Maggie hedged, looking away from Dahlia, who was always too good at seeing to the heart of things.


“Did he tell you what happened that day?”


Maggie bit her lip. “He was interrupted during the incantation. A family emergency,” Maggie explained, but she didn’t give any additional details. That wasn’t her story to tell. “It wasn’t what I thought it was.”


“Huh,” was all Dahlia said in return. She popped the last bite of croissant in her mouth, balled up the bag, and threw it in the trash. Dahlia had the same expression on her face as when she was trying to work out a difficult rune, and Maggie waited for her to say something snarky about Taliesin, but instead, she said, “Oh! I heard from Rodrigo last night.”


Maggie brightened. “How is he? Have there been any more ghoul sightings?”


“No, everything has been quiet. He only called to tell me he hasn’t seen anyone fitting the description of your mystery man, yet.”


She realized then that she hadn’t thought about the Beltane kiss except in passing in days. It had so consumed her thoughts after it happened. She wasn’t as invested in finding him as Dahlia was, but even still, the memory of the heat of that kiss, of the way her heart had beat faster as they’d danced, would come to her unbidden, derailing whatever she was doing. But something had changed. Maybe some of the shine had worn off now that she had other things occupying her mind.


She didn’t want to admit, not to Dahlia and certainly not to herself, that maybe she hadn’t thought about the Beltane kiss because of the strange electricity between her and Taliesin. There wasn’t room for two men in her brain, and, infuriatingly, Taliesin was taking up all the space. And if, maybe once or twice, she’d wondered how he kissed, that wasn’t her fault when she caught him staring at her the way he did.


“Maybe it’s for the best,” was all she said to Dahlia, with an indifferent shrug. “I haven’t thought about Beltane in a while. It’s just not in the stars for me and the mystery man, I guess.”


Her friend wasn’t one to let things go unsaid, but Maggie had the distinct impression that Dahlia was holding back when all she said was, “Interesting,” one last time as she returned Maggie’s file folder of runes to her.



—


Maggie ended her last class of the day fifteen minutes early. “Remember,” she told her students as they packed up their belongings, “you will need fresh chalk for your final next week. Please bring pure chalk—no enhancing decoctions are allowed.” She would remind them again by email next week, but still every year someone tried to use chalk mixed with silver dust or moon water. Neither of those additions would do anything to help a student who hadn’t studied, but it didn’t mean they weren’t going to try.


Maggie almost convinced herself that ending her class fifteen minutes early was a gift to her students—a little extra time for them to cram for another class, finish last-minute coursework, or just rest—but truthfully, it gave Maggie time to snoop before she had to meet Taliesin. When she was sure that none of her students had any pre-finals questions, she said hasty goodbyes and left for the south staircase.


Ilex Hall had its quirks since it began its life as a manor house, built at the edge of the Wilds by an eccentric architect and philanthropist when Galloway was nothing more than a few farms. He had intentionally built the manor to be an observation point for the Wilds, with wide, tall windows on the upper floors and covered brick walkways that dipped into the edge of the forest. In the center of the building was a large courtyard, where plants found within the Wilds were once cultivated and observed.


Now the courtyards and gardens on campus doubled as teaching plots for the Botany and Mycology Department. Some of them were still relegated as observational plots for local flora, but the courtyard in Ilex Hall, due to its proximity to the alchemy labs, was full to bursting with plants that could be used in the decoctions added to chalk to enhance runes. Vervain and yew were for many things but primarily warding spellwork that repelled or banished fantasmia; wormwood and mugwort were for scrying and other, murkier divination spells; mountain laurel and wild aster were frequently employed as a calming decoction for spellwork with unfavorable astrology or other sticky details. They could reduce the likelihood of a pall, and early career alchemists often relied on them. If only Taliesin still had his chalk training wheels on.


The northern staircase was still cordoned off since it had been contaminated with pall slime, meaning students and faculty were crowded in the southern staircase in between each class. It also meant that Maggie would be on the wrong side of the building to Taliesin’s Materials Alchemy lab, so she decided to cut through the courtyard.


The path coiled through the courtyard like a nautilus, converging on a small, flowering hawthorn tree in the center. The beds were neat and orderly, with the electric green of new spring growth and blooms bursting forth in pinks, whites, and purples. The campus gardeners, worried about the gloom cast by the pall and the reduced sunlight, had installed small lights shaped like wide leaves to help the plants grow. The lights vined through the courtyard garden like a lucent pothos, creating a dazzling array that seemed to have grown overnight. The strangely festive, twinkling glow left Maggie breathless.


Maggie cut through the garden on stepping stones, brushing her hand across a soft reaching sweet fern, until she stood outside Taliesin’s class. Materials Alchemy had been relocated from a third-floor lab to this cramped classroom tucked off the courtyard near the northern staircase. Even though the room was small, it had tall windows and a back door that opened to the garden. Most professors who taught in that classroom kept the door open since the room was so small and stuffy, letting in a little bit of cool, fresh air. She was pleased to find that Taliesin had done the same.


Through the open door, Maggie had a view of about half the students and Taliesin by the chalkboard. She knew it was the same class that had experienced the pall, and she recognized most of the students, if not from her own classes, then from helping them down the stairs to safety that day. Materials Alchemy had a reputation for being a chore of a class. At Hawthorn, it was previously taught by an ancient professor who had finally retired last spring. The coursework consisted of basic lessons on the transformation of organic and inorganic materials, an essential building block for many complicated spells. Maggie was surprised when Taliesin was hired specifically to teach it. He taught three Materials Alchemy labs and then two other slightly more advanced intro courses. She would have expected such a famous visiting scholar to teach more advanced, niche topics, but this was just another way that Taliesin surprised her.


Maggie pulled her sweater tighter over her shoulders as she peeked through the door of Taliesin’s class. Up at the front of the room, she saw a different version of him than any she had met so far. Taliesin bounded around from the chalkboard to the lectern to directly in front of his students’ desks without any of the awkwardness she had seen on the auditorium stage. He was energetic. Enthusiastic. On the board, he had drawn an example of a complicated rune. Maggie’s materials alchemy was rusty, but it looked like the conversion of iron into copper.


Maggie didn’t hear the question Taliesin asked or his student’s answer, but she saw the triumphant grin on his face as he exclaimed, “Yes, exactly!” and turned to make a note on the chalkboard in scratchy handwriting. His students now chattered over each other, and Maggie braced herself for Taliesin to lose his cool, but he didn’t. “One at a time!” he urged calmly, and the chatter stopped.


The students shouted out ideas, one at a time as Taliesin had requested, and he marked them on the board, nodding or gently correcting, steering the discussion effortlessly. Of the students Maggie could see, they all watched him with rapt attention, and most joined in the discussion and took notes. Gods above, is he a good teacher, too?


Maggie would have liked to blame his students’ enthusiasm on Taliesin’s fame, but students could usually see right through that, especially after the first few classes. It was very clear to her that he was good at this and that he liked it, too. And though they certainly had differences in opinion about the how, it was obvious that Taliesin loved his job in much the same way that Maggie did.


Abruptly, Taliesin looked up at the clock in the room, which was inconveniently right above the doorway Maggie peeked through. She didn’t have time to duck out of view and instead offered up a sheepish half wave. Taliesin gave her a wry grin before saying to his class, “Time’s up! Bring this same energy to your final and you’ll all do fine.”


He paused and then added, “I know some of you might have tried to find me during office hours last week. I was ill and missed them, I’m sorry about that—if you tried to come talk to me, shoot me an email and we’ll set up a one-on-one.”


Maggie didn’t know how he would have time for that, but she had no doubt that he’d scrounge some up. He began erasing the chalkboard as his students filed out, some of them lining up to talk to Taliesin. The rest left through the courtyard, cutting a faster path to some of the dorms on the south side of campus. She smiled warmly and waved hello as they passed while she waited for Taliesin to finish talking to his students.


Unlike Maggie, he didn’t rush out of his room to join her, but she did catch him sneaking glances at her. She tried to appear busy, spending far more time looking at the new garden lights than necessary.


Maggie’s stomach fluttered every time she caught Taliesin looking at her with those kind brown eyes, a light, dizzy sensation that unsettled her. She had felt it last night, with their legs twined together in the window seat at Willoughby’s, as he’d listened to her so intently while she’d told him some version of the truth about her first year in Galloway. She wasn’t even sure why she’d told him any of it, only that she wanted to share a piece of herself after he’d shared so much of himself.


But now, the fluttering feeling curdled slightly. It all reminded her too much of her ex, of Evan, of the way they’d cast hurried glances at each other over textbooks, across labs, like they were the only two people in the world. The final time her eyes met Taliesin’s, he gave her one of those smiles that crinkled the corners of his eyes. It was too much, and Maggie was desperate to keep it from happening again.

facts.fact: 道歉羊角包开场：她自以为若无其事被 Dahlia 立刻看穿。
coffee coffee 测谎：语言学家被 reduplication 逼供，只能承认 working coffee。
招供内幕：上周五、以独自进 pall 采数据威胁入伙；Dahlia 复述成用涉险换帮助。
facts.anchor: I told him I would enter the pall for myself

facts.fact: 她的诊断：病理性内疚+也许恋母；Dahlia 接梗换我妈是 Rowena 我也会有。
守密原则：Least of all you 烙在记忆里——有些东西留给自己；对 Dahlia 隐去 Lane（不是她的故事）。
facts.anchor: That wasn’t her story to tell.

facts.fact: 脑内没有两个男人的空间：Taliesin 占满；神秘人搜索降温（Rodrigo 无斩获）。
facts.anchor: There wasn’t room for two men in her brain

facts.fact: 期末规则：final 用纯净粉笔，不许银尘/月水增强。
Ilex Hall 身世：观景宅邸（高层大窗+砖廊探林）；中庭植物分栏（vervain/yew 护界、苦艾 scrying）。
facts.anchor: an observation point for the Wilds

facts.fact: 偷课实录：他满场飞、稳住抢答（One at a time!）——她惊他连课都教得好。
facts.anchor: Taliesin bounded around from the chalkboard

facts.fact: 结尾警报：急促对视像极 Evan 时代——雀跃感 curdled；她怕重蹈覆辙。
